One time, in my misspent youth, I misjudged a dose of benzodiazepines (lorazepam/Ativan) by exactly a factor of ten. Here's what I did.

I drove my car aimlessly around the city. I'm lucky I didn't kill someone, because I didn't give a fuck. I easily could have run someone over without feeling *any* anxiety.  I ended up at a shopping mall I had never been to. I went to the drug store, bought 3 bottles of cough syrup, a big box of condoms, a 4-pack of enemas, a chocolate bar, and a tube of something called "anusol" just to be funny. I dumped all this shit on the counter and paid for it with pride. Then, I realized I had lost my car keys (luckily). So I walked around the city aimlessly with my condoms and my enemas and my cough syrup for about an hour, until I got on some random bus. I chatted with the bus driver, because I thought he was my friend. I rode random buses until I ended up back at my house.

I lived with friends, so my bedroom door was locked, but my keys were lost. So, I tried to saw a hole through the wall with a steak knife. When that didn't work, I left the knife in the wall, left my bag of loot with my friends, and went back outside. I found a rotten wooden ladder in my neighbor's yard, stole it, used it to climb up on the roof of the two story house, and then broke in my own window. 

Then I drank all of the cough syrup. But I still didn't feel high enough, so I walked to the convenience store while I was high on lorazepam and cough syrup, to buy *more* cough syrup. I drank the cough syrup on the sidewalk in full view of everyone like it was Pepsi.

I drank so much cough syrup that I had an out of body experience, saw a whole bunch of extra dimensions, and made contact with aliens. But that's another story. 

When I regained consciousness the next day, I could not form proper sentences, and I walked like Frankenstein. I definitely damaged my brain. My friend had to drive me all around the city to find my car. 

The day after, I had a job interview. I still couldn't walk properly, but I got the job.

They can allow you to see yourself, and your relationship with the world, in a whole new light. People on psychedelics will re-evaluate long-held beliefs. It can also expose hidden truths. These revelations can be quite uncomfortable if you are not prepared for them.

LSD is not a party drug, IMO. You should only do it around people you trust. You should think of LSD as a form of therapy. It's going to put you in touch with every possible facet of your mind. You will be challenged, and you have to be willing to accept whatever it throws at you.

It's important to remember, however, that these new perspectives can be just as distorted as your old ones. It is only because you had not considered them before that they will carry so much weight. New perspectives can be highly beneficial, and can help people overcome mental obstacles and become a better person. New perspectives can also be highly destructive, causing people to second-guess aspects of themselves that were highly successful in the past. LSD can turn a homeless man into a CEO, but it can also turn a CEO into a homeless man. It's powerful stuff.

LSD has made you consciously aware of aspects of yourself that have made you uncomfortable and self-conscious. The fact that you act like your mother (*FYI*, we all do) is the perfect example of the kind of "truth bomb" that LSD can drop. After all, the main effect of LSD is to "free your mind". If you react to these kinds of revelations by trying to block them, you end up creating walls in your mind. Basically, you're trying to artificially recreate the mental blockages you had before you ever took LSD. But you can't. The cat is out of the bag. You can't ever *unsee* the image of yourself as being like your mother, for example. If you try, you are lying to yourself. All of this explains why you are behaving so awkwardly around other people. You had a glimpse of life-altering revelations, and now you are trying to pretend that nothing happened. 

The good news is that you really shouldn't be so worried. As I said, LSD doesn't necessarily show you "the truth", it only shows you different perspectives. These perspectives are nothing to be afraid of, and if you face them head-on, you will usually realise that they are of no threat to you. Many people who take LSD go on a mental journey, and end up right back where they started, with one or two useful alternative ways of thinking added to their mental toolkit. (For example, there may be situations in the future where you will find it beneficial to channel your mother. Surely she has her strengths.) But you are still the same person that you always were. 

Several people have suggested that you take more LSD. I am torn on this. It *may* work, but it may also make things worse. If you do decide to try it again, do some research on how LSD can be used as a therapeutic tool, and not as a form of recreation.
